questions.q: What Sentinel object decides WHEN an action like running a playbook actually happens?
options: An automation rule
The Log Analytics workspace
The playbook itself, by checking its own trigger conditions
A KQL hunting query
questions.explain: The automation rule is the separate object whose entire job is deciding when a playbook or other action should run.

questions.q: What are the two real trigger types an automation rule can fire on?
options: When incident is created, and when incident is updated
When a log arrives, and when a log is deleted
When a user logs in, and when a user logs out
Daily and weekly, on a fixed schedule only
questions.explain: An automation rule fires either once at incident creation, or every time an existing incident is later updated.

questions.q: What does a condition do inside an automation rule?
options: Narrows which incidents qualify, based on properties like severity, title, or tags
Changes the playbook's Logic App designer layout
Sets how long logs are retained in the workspace
Converts a hunting query into a scheduled analytics rule
questions.explain: A trigger alone fires on every incident; a condition is the if/then logic that narrows it to the subset you actually mean.

questions.q: In the division of labor between an automation rule and a playbook, which statement is accurate?
options: The rule decides when an action happens; the playbook decides what actually happens
The playbook decides when to run; the rule decides what happens inside the workflow
Rules and playbooks are the same object with two different names
A playbook can exist without ever being connected to any automation rule's action
questions.explain: Keeping 'when' (the rule) separate from 'what' (the playbook) is what makes the system composable and reusable.

questions.q: Why does keeping the automation rule and the playbook as two separate objects matter in practice?
options: The same playbook can be reused by several different rules, each with its own trigger condition
It has no practical benefit — it's purely how Sentinel's UI happens to be organized
It means a playbook can only ever be triggered by exactly one automation rule
It removes the need for a Microsoft Sentinel connector inside the Logic App
questions.explain: Because the condition lives in the rule, you can point one playbook at a phishing rule and a brute-force rule without rebuilding the workflow.
